messages.subject: Re: [unmarked] manually fixing parameters?
messages.body_plain:
This will eventually be implemented but I can't say when. In the
meantime, a crude workaround is to use offset(). Following the occu
example:

(fm <- occu(~ offset(-0.00589*obsvar1) ~ 1, pferUMF))

offsets currently don't work in colext, and it might not warn. This
will be fixed in the next release.

Richard

messages.body_plain:
Hi Imran,

I tried this and it seems to work fine:

library(unmarked)
fha <- read.csv("D:/R/Scripts/unmarkedHelp/Imran/fha_data.csv", header=TRUE)
levels(fha$Tr) <- c(levels(fha$Tr), "TR1", "TR7", "TR9", "TR15",
"TR17", "TR18")
db <- c(0, 5, 10, 15, 25, 40,55, 70, 75)
fha.y <- formatDistData(fha, distCol="PDIST", transectNameCol="Tr",
     dist.breaks=db)
umf <- unmarkedFrameDS(y = as.matrix(fha.y), survey="line",
     dist.breaks=db, tlength=rep(100, 18), unitsI="m")
hist(umf)

fm1 <- distsamp(~1 ~1, umf)
summary(fm1)
backTransform(fm1, type="state") # Density = 1.36/ha
hist(fm1)

What is wrong with 1.36/ha? Seems reasonable based upon an observed
density of:

20/(100*75*2*18/10000) # = 0.74/ha

As for your covariate models, I don't have your data and the covs1
object in your script only has covariates for 12 transects, and I
assume you don't want to throw away the other 6. It looks like you are
using backTransform and linearComb incorrectly. You need to provide
covariate values for each covariate in the model. In your examples you
use c(0, 5), which doesn't make sense to me. Normally you will have an
intercept so the first value should be 1. An alternative is to use the
predict() method, which is described on various help pages and in the
distance sampling vignette:

vignette("distsamp")

I'm afraid I don't have much more time to commit to this, but perhaps
other folks on the list can contribute.

Richard

messages.subject: Re: Unmarked Covariate modeling
messages.body_plain:
Glad to help. As Andy pointed out, cluster size will likely affect
detection probability so distsamp may not be appropriate for your
data. As for the higher density estimate from DISTANCE, it could be
due to cluster size but you should make sure that you told that
program how much area you surveyed. By default I believe that it
ignores transects where no individuals were detected.

Richard

What is wrong with 1.36/ha? Seems reasonable based upon an observed density
of:

20/(100*75*2*18/10000) # = 0.74/ha

As for your covariate models, I don't have your data and the covs1 object
in your script only has covariates for 12 transects, and I assume you don't
want to throw away the other 6. It looks like you are using backTransform
and linearComb incorrectly. You need to provide covariate values for each
covariate in the model. In your examples you use c(0, 5), which doesn't make
sense to me. Normally you will have an intercept so the first value should
be 1. An alternative is to use the predict() method, which is described on
various help pages and in the distance sampling vignette:

vignette("distsamp")

Hi Imran,

Cluster size is an important issue that has not been addressed yet in
unmarked. Cluster size is not a transect-specific covariate, so it
might be difficult to formally include in this model. However, I think
you could model the abundance of clusters and then multiply your
*cluster abundance* estimate by the average number of individuals per
cluster to get a post-hoc estimate of population size. Let me think
more about this.

Could you be more specific about what you mean by effort? If you used
line-transects, you can specify the length of each transect in your
call to unmarkedFrameDS, which will account for that type of variation
in effort. Other types of variation in effort could be modeled as
covariates or included as a priori known effects using the offset()
function in your formula.

I'm not quite sure what you mean in your third question. If you have
multiple covariates, you can use a model selection process to find the
best model. If they are highly correlated, you could use PCA and then
include the PCs as covariates.

It is not currently possible to do multispecies model.

Here is some code that might help (I don't have your data so I can't
test this):

# Bin the data to create a response matrix
cuts <- seq(0, 100, by=10) # or something like c(10, 30, 60, 100)
y <- formatDistData(fha, "Dist", "TR", cuts) # Note that I used "TR"
and not "Clusters"

# Make sure the rows for the response are in the same order as your
covariate data
y <- y[rownames(covs1),]

# Create unmarkedFrame, assuming you have line-transect data recorded
in meters and
# transect lengths are the same.
umf <- unmarkedFrameDS(y=y, siteCovs=as.data.frame(covs1),
survey="line", unitsIn="m")

# Fit a model
m1 <- distsamp(~1 ~habitat, umf, keyfun="halfnorm", output="abund")

The first thing to do it to decide which model you would like to use.
Do
you want to model presence absence data, or do you want to model
abundance?

most
likely want to model abundance/density. Is this correct? If so, you
should
check out the distsamp function, which allows you to include
covariates
affecting abundance and detection probability. This model assumes a
multinomial distribution for the response variable, so you must bin
the
data
into distance intervals. Binning you data, if done carefully, should
not
affect limit you ability to detect patterns in your data. Please see
the
help page for the function formatDistData. This function makes it easy
to
bin data and to try various distance cut points.

data.
